{{Short description|none}}
{{Electromagnetism|Covariance}}

In [[relativistic physics]], the '''electromagnetic stress–energy tensor''' is the contribution to the [[stress–energy tensor]] due to the [[electromagnetic field]].<ref name="WheelerEtAl">Gravitation, J.A. Wheeler, C. Misner, K.S. Thorne, W.H. Freeman & Co, 1973, {{ISBN|0-7167-0344-0}}</ref> The stress–energy tensor describes the flow of energy and momentum in [[spacetime]]. The electromagnetic stress–energy tensor contains the negative of the classical [[Maxwell stress tensor]] that governs the electromagnetic interactions.

It was introduced by [[Hermann Minkowski]] in 1907.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ni |first=Wei-tou |url=https://www.google.fr/books/edition/One_Hundred_Years_Of_General_Relativity/lvUnDwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=electromagnetic+stress+energy+minkowski+1907+history&pg=PA91&printsec=frontcover |title=One Hundred Years Of General Relativity: From Genesis And Empirical Foundations To Gravitational Waves, Cosmology And Quantum Gravity - Volume 1 |date=2017-05-26 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-4635-14-1 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Die Grundgleichungen für die elektromagnetischen Vorgänge in bewegten Körpern – Wikisource |url=https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Grundgleichungen_f%C3%BCr_die_elektromagnetischen_Vorg%C3%A4nge_in_bewegten_K%C3%B6rpern |access-date=2026-05-21 |website=de.wikisource.org |language=de}}</ref>

== Definition ==

=== ISQ convention ===

The electromagnetic stress–energy tensor in the [[International System of Quantities]] (ISQ), which underlies the [[SI]], is<ref name="WheelerEtAl"/>
<math display="block">T^{\mu\nu} = \frac{1}{\mu_0} \left[ F^{\mu \alpha}F^\nu{}_{\alpha} - \frac{1}{4} \eta^{\mu\nu}F_{\alpha\beta} F^{\alpha\beta}\right] \,,</math>
where <math>F^{\mu\nu}</math> is the [[electromagnetic tensor]] and where <math>\eta_{\mu\nu}</math> is the [[Metric tensor (general relativity)#Flat spacetime|Minkowski metric tensor]] of [[metric signature]] {{nowrap|(− + + +)}} and the [[Einstein summation convention]] over repeated indices is used.

Explicitly in matrix form:
<math display="block">T^{\mu\nu} = \begin{bmatrix}
  u & \frac{1}{c}S_\text{x} & \frac{1}{c}S_\text{y} & \frac{1}{c}S_\text{z} \\
  \frac{1}{c}S_\text{x} & -\sigma_\text{xx} & -\sigma_\text{xy} & -\sigma_\text{xz} \\
  \frac{1}{c}S_\text{y} & -\sigma_\text{yx} & -\sigma_\text{yy} & -\sigma_\text{yz} \\
  \frac{1}{c}S_\text{z} & -\sigma_\text{zx} & -\sigma_\text{zy} & -\sigma_\text{zz}
\end{bmatrix},</math>
where
<math display="block">u = \frac{1}{2}\left(\epsilon_0 \mathbf{E}^2+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{B}^2\right)</math>
is the volumetric energy density,
<math display="block">\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}</math>
is the [[Poynting vector]], 
<math display="block">\sigma_{ij} = \epsilon_0 E_i E_j + \frac{1}{{\mu _0}}B_i B_j - \frac{1}{2} \left( \epsilon_0 \mathbf{E}^2 + \frac{1}{\mu _0}\mathbf{B}^2 \right)\delta _{ij} </math>
is the [[Maxwell stress tensor]], and <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]]. Thus, each component of <math>T^{\mu\nu}</math> is dimensionally equivalent to pressure (with SI unit [[Pascal (unit)|pascal]]).

=== Gaussian CGS conventions ===

The constants in the [[Gaussian units|Gaussian system]] (shown here with a prime) that correspond to the [[permittivity of free space]] and [[permeability of free space]] are
<math display="block">\epsilon_0' = \frac{1}{4\pi},\quad \mu_0' = 4\pi</math>
then:
<math display="block">T^{\mu\nu} = \frac{1}{4\pi} \left[F'^{\mu\alpha}F'^{\nu}{}_{\alpha} - \frac{1}{4} \eta^{\mu\nu}F'_{\alpha\beta}F'^{\alpha\beta}\right] </math>
and in explicit matrix form:
<math display="block">T^{\mu\nu} = \begin{bmatrix}
  u & \frac{1}{c}S_\text{x} & \frac{1}{c}S_\text{y} & \frac{1}{c}S_\text{z} \\
  \frac{1}{c}S_\text{x} & -\sigma_\text{xx} & -\sigma_\text{xy} & -\sigma_\text{xz} \\
  \frac{1}{c}S_\text{y} & -\sigma_\text{yx} & -\sigma_\text{yy} & -\sigma_\text{yz} \\
  \frac{1}{c}S_\text{z} & -\sigma_\text{zx} & -\sigma_\text{zy} & -\sigma_\text{zz}
\end{bmatrix}</math>
where the energy density becomes
<math display="block">u = \frac{1}{8\pi}\left(\mathbf{E}'^2 + \mathbf{B}'^2\right)</math>
and the [[Poynting vector]] becomes 
<math display="block">\mathbf{S} = \frac{c}{4\pi}\mathbf{E}'\times\mathbf{B}'.</math>

The stress–energy tensor for an electromagnetic field in a [[dielectric]] medium is less well understood and is the subject of the [[Abraham–Minkowski controversy]].<ref>however see Pfeifer et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 79, 1197 (2007)</ref>

The element <math>T^{\mu\nu}</math> of the stress–energy tensor represents the flux of the component with index <math>\mu</math> of the [[four-momentum]] of the electromagnetic field, {{tmath|1= P^{\mu} }}, going through a [[hyperplane]]. It represents the contribution of electromagnetism to the source of the gravitational field (curvature of spacetime) in [[general relativity]].

== Algebraic properties ==
The electromagnetic stress–energy tensor has several algebraic properties:
{{unordered list
| It is a [[symmetric tensor]]:
<math display="block">T^{\mu\nu} = T^{\nu\mu}</math> 
| The tensor <math>T^{\nu}{}_{\alpha}</math> is [[Trace (linear algebra)|traceless]] (in 4D):
<math display="block">T^{\alpha}{}_{\alpha} = 0.</math>

{{math proof
|proof = Starting with
<math display="block">T^{\mu}{}_{\mu} = \eta_{\mu\nu}T^{\mu\nu}</math>

Using the explicit form of the tensor,
<math display="block">T^{\mu}{}_{\mu} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left[\eta_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\alpha}F^{\nu}{}_{\alpha} - \eta_{\mu\nu}\eta^{\mu\nu}\frac{1}{4}F^{\alpha\beta}F_{\alpha\beta}\right]</math>

Lowering the indices and using the fact that {{tmath|1= \eta^{\mu\nu}\eta_{\mu\nu} = \delta^{\mu}_{\mu} }},
<math display="block">T^{\mu}{}_{\mu} = \frac{1}{\mu_0} \left[F^{\mu\alpha} F_{\mu\alpha} - \delta^{\mu}_{\mu} \frac{1}{4} F^{\alpha\beta} F_{\alpha\beta}\right]</math>

Then, using {{tmath|1= \delta^{\mu}_{\mu} = 4 }},
<math display="block">T^{\mu}{}_{\mu} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left[F^{\mu\alpha} F_{\mu\alpha} - F^{\alpha\beta} F_{\alpha\beta}\right]</math>

Note that in the first term, <math>\mu</math> and <math>\alpha</math> are dummy indices, so we relabel them as <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> respectively.
<math display="block">T^{\alpha}{}_{\alpha} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left[F^{\alpha\beta} F_{\alpha\beta} - F^{\alpha\beta} F_{\alpha\beta}\right] = 0</math>
}}
| The energy density is [[Positive-definite function|positive-definite]]:
<math display="block">T^{00} \ge 0</math>
}}

The symmetry of the tensor is as for a general stress–energy tensor in [[general relativity]]. The trace of the energy–momentum tensor is a [[Lorentz scalar]]; the electromagnetic field (and in particular electromagnetic waves) has no [[Lorentz transformation|Lorentz-invariant]] energy scale, so its energy–momentum tensor must have a vanishing trace. This tracelessness eventually relates to the masslessness of the [[photon]].<ref>Garg, Anupam. ''Classical Electromagnetism in a Nutshell'', p. 564 (Princeton University Press, 2012).</ref>

== Conservation laws ==
{{further|Conservation laws}}

The electromagnetic stress–energy tensor allows a compact way of writing the [[conservation laws]] of linear [[momentum]] and [[energy]] in electromagnetism. The divergence of the stress–energy tensor is:
<math display="block">\partial_\nu T^{\mu \nu} + \eta^{\mu \rho} \, f_\rho = 0 \,</math>
where <math>f_\rho</math> is the (4D) [[Lorentz force]] per unit volume on [[matter]].

This equation is equivalent to the following 3D conservation laws
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \frac{\partial u_\mathrm{em}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{J} \cdot \mathbf{E} &= 0 \\
  \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}_\mathrm{em}}{\partial t} - \mathbf{\nabla}\cdot \sigma + \rho \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B} &= 0
    \ \Leftrightarrow\ \epsilon_0 \mu_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{S}}{\partial t} - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{\sigma} + \mathbf{f} = 0
\end{align}</math>
respectively describing the electromagnetic energy density
<math display="block">u_\mathrm{em} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \epsilon_0\mathbf{E}^2 + \frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{B}^2 \right) </math>
and electromagnetic momentum density 
<math display="block">\mathbf{p}_\mathrm{em} = {\mathbf{S} \over {c^2}} ,</math>
where <math>\mathbf{J}</math> is the [[electric current density]], <math>\rho</math> the [[electric charge density]], and <math>\mathbf{f} </math> is the Lorentz force density.
